intuition: Push something and it speeds up. The **same push** moves a light thing easily and a heavy thing barely — the acceleration $a$ you get is the force $F$ divided by the mass $m$. Buying that push costs effort, not \$5 bills.
why: This single line turns forces into *predictions of motion* — the engine of classical mechanics.

widget.title: Feel the trade-off between force, mass and acceleration

example.setup: A trolley has mass $m = 12\ \text{kg}$ and you want $a = 1.5\ \text{m/s}^2$.

applications: Car crumple zones lengthen a crash, lowering $a$ and the force on passengers.
Rocket engineers balance thrust against ever-decreasing fuel mass.
A golfer maximizes club-head force on a low-mass ball.
history: Isaac Newton published the three laws of motion in the *Principia* in 1687.
derivation: Newton's general statement is $F = \dfrac{dp}{dt}$ with momentum $p = mv$.
